# One Connect: multiple projects, native workspace and Docker databases

You are the implementation worker for this subsystem. Work only inside this isolated workspace. The coordinator will integrate your diff with two other workers. Implement working features, usable UI and meaningful tests.

Read docs/one-connect.md, docs/desktop.md, docs/one-answer.md, packages/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs and terminal.rs, daemon/context, docker.ts, paths/config/server/http.ts and web Workspace/desktop bridge/App. Baseline passes 133 tests. One Answer already ingests redacted exact Git snapshots automatically, with explicit partial status and private default vault.

Deliver:
1. Durable project registry and a Mac-first add/switch/manage project interface. Select a local repository from a native folder picker or prepare cloning from a Git URL. Validate exact project binding and isolate databases, dashboards, indexes, agent definitions, Docker namespaces and terminal directories. Do not lose project state on restart. Avoid opening unrelated folders. New-project onboarding should identify declared checks/frameworks/container services without executing scripts. Wire successful additions to One Answer indexing and show intake status. For uncommitted/uninitialized local projects, give an explicit safe onboarding step rather than pretend they are indexed at a Git SHA.
2. Switching projects should keep separate supervisors and live agent runs running; returning restores their dashboard/logs. Each terminal belongs to its project. Provide per-project stop and global kill controls. Fix current desktop limitation which refuses all switching while any run is active. Secure IPC/request routing must bind a project identity and its auth connection; never mix tokens, responses or WS state across projects. Graceful shutdown and restart recovery for every project.
3. Project Docker workbench: detect Docker availability, show project-owned containers/services/status and logs, start/stop/restart/build using exact project Compose binding and expiring action-bound human decisions. Do not stop unrelated containers. A local database wizard for Postgres and optionally SQLite should generate project-owned files and a reviewable command/Compose plan, then launch approved steps from the in-app terminal/control. No automatic image pulls/network before the user approves the exact action. Keep passwords out of prompts/logs/tracker and use secrets/local generated files with restrictive permissions. Never touch a production database.
4. Health/verification: honest readiness from actual healthchecks, bounded log output, image/pull/port conflicts surfaced, database state survives restart via scoped Docker volume. Provide command preview, connection info with credentials hidden, and terminal launch action. Use disposable Docker protocol fixtures, not the user's running services; real Docker smoke testing only if images already present and disposable scope clearly recorded.

Integration contract: prefer a native project registry module and isolated core/daemon project/environment modules; localize main.rs/Desktop bridge/App/Workspace edits. Other workers touch routes/config, so describe integration points clearly. Preserve One Answer, Designer, tracker adapters and custom agents. Existing acc commands and app-data identifier remain compatible. Keep SPDX Apache-2.0 and no new dependency/lockfile changes without asking coordinator. Only project apps/tests/services run in Docker; agent provider harnesses and supervisor stay native.

Safety: official subscription harness only; human confirmed Cursor on-demand OFF. Do not use APIs, paid fallback, change billing/login, install packages/images, access unrelated personal paths or apps, run another agent, push/publish/deploy, send outbound messages, make production DB writes or activate a live Git/tracker/infra integration. Code for cloning must gate the exact outbound action through human approval; your implementation tests use local Git repositories. Read installed node_modules through supplied links, never edit them or original repo. Run installed tooling only in this workspace/disposable fixtures; Cargo offline checks are allowed, don't accept any Xcode/license prompts.

Run pnpm typecheck and focused vitest/Rust checks appropriate to changes. Finish HANDOFF.md with files, behavior, exact commands and actual results, remaining gaps and shared-file integration points. No commit required. If blocked, state the concrete blocker and complete unaffected work. No silent model downgrade or usage-limit retry.

# One Connect product architecture

## Confirmed product choices

One Connect is a Mac-first application that joins the development cycle across vendors. The Tauri/Rust shell, supervisor, official subscription harnesses and optional API harness run natively. Only the project being developed runs in Docker: its apps, services, databases, development tools and checks. Later Windows support shares the portable UI and core, with platform-specific process and permission validation.

Ask your docs means semantic search and grounded questions over the user's selected Obsidian folders. Jev means TypeSafe's System One model. Jev may recommend, classify urgency and decide when to escalate; it cannot record a human approval. Its metered connection remains disabled until the owner explicitly enables it. Mock design means editable interactive previews and a versioned design system that implementation and review must follow; Figma is outside the initial design scope.

### One Answer intake

Every added project, whether cloned from Git or selected locally, receives a revision-bound project scan. Extract repository structure, language/framework inventory, manifest dependencies, declared checks and container services, source documentation and architecture references without executing project scripts. Exclude secrets, binary/generated/vendor files and symlinks; report indexing limits explicitly. Write cited notes into the selected Obsidian project folder (a private local markdown vault before an Obsidian connection is selected), index them with local embeddings when enabled, and build the Graphify graph from the same Git revision. Track each component's revision and freshness separately; One Answer must flag a partial or stale scan rather than promise omniscience. Agents and the human query this same retrieval layer. Source changes refresh the derived notes/index/graph, not another independent copy of project truth.

### Designer defaults

The designer includes pinned Taste Skill and Vercel Web Interface Guidelines text, licensed DESIGN.md references, a scoped Playwright CLI integration guide, and original skills for accessible UI, responsive mocks and design-contract enforcement. Open Design (`nexu-io/open-design`) is a reviewed Apache-2.0 reference implementation; reuse selected resources with source commits and upstream MIT notices. Keep hosted plans, telemetry, media APIs and executable installations disabled. Load skill descriptions cheaply and detailed references on demand. Every project design system has validated tokens, rules, a version/hash, preview and DESIGN.md/CSS exports. Assignments freeze that revision so implementation and review see the same contract.

## Components and sources of truth

- Rust owns the native window, terminal, project registry, private daemon connection and OS integration. Keep the working TypeScript supervisor until measurements justify moving a specific hot path to Rust.
- Each project has an isolated SQLite event store, tracker binding, policies, worktrees, Docker Compose namespace, context index and dashboard. Git owns code; the tracker owns issue state; the event log owns actions, runs, messages and human decisions.
- The supervisor runs official vendor harnesses for subscriptions. API mode uses an independently licensed open-source harness behind the same adapter interface, never a subscription session token. Select and pin that harness after contract tests for streaming, approvals, tools, restart and container access.
- All clients share the same typed reducer and receive live event updates. Logs survive restarts. A complete message or test claim is never replaced by an attractive preview.

## Agent coordination

One project-scoped message bus carries targeted questions, replies, blockers and handoffs. Every message has a sender, recipients, issue/run references, optional reply link and durable acknowledgements. A dashboard shows the same messages agents see. Authenticated run tokens determine the sender; agents cannot impersonate another agent or read another project's inbox.

At dispatch, every agent receives a compact current team snapshot: agent roles, Now/Next, ownership and path scopes, pending decisions and its own unread message identifiers. During a run, agents pull `get_team` and `read_messages`, and use `send_team_message` when coordination is needed. Streaming harnesses receive a small inbox notification, not everyone else's transcripts. Harnesses without live input pull at tool boundaries; message state stays durable until acknowledged. A notification never creates an unapproved new run or paid call.

Shared state prevents stale ownership; dependency edges and independent review prevent simultaneous incompatible work. Agents communicate advice and evidence, not authority to override cost, security, path or release policies. The human can inspect and answer any thread. A coordinator coordinates through tools rather than driving other apps.

## Context and token efficiency

Combine scoped Obsidian retrieval with Graphify's code graph. Store content hashes and index incrementally. Retrieve small cited passages, load skill instructions only when used, and send event/state deltas rather than transcript broadcasts. Label character-derived token estimates as estimates; provider-reported token usage is separate. Quality is evaluated through acceptance checks, independent review and a retrieval evaluation set, never inferred from fewer tokens.

Evaluate QMD and permissively licensed Obsidian semantic-search implementations for local embeddings and hybrid retrieval. No unrelated vault folders, symlink escapes, remote embeddings or automatic model downloads. Ask your docs answers must cite retrieved note passages and say when no evidence was found.

## Phased delivery and verification

1. **Connected workspace:** One Connect identity, project-scoped durable communication, compact team snapshots, message dashboard, token/idle/run analytics and current-state evidence. Verify authenticated agent-to-agent exchange, replies, acknowledgement, redaction, bounded context, live UI updates and replay after restart.
2. **Build a team:** custom agents, shared provider capacity, skills and connector management, coordinated/independent workflow execution, multi-project registry and dashboards. Verify parallel worktrees, queue recovery, provider limits, connector isolation and workflow dependencies.
3. **Design and development:** interactive mock builder, design-system artifacts and enforcement, scoped semantic vault retrieval/Q&A, Graphify context metrics, official provider streaming/approval protocols and chosen API harness. Verify real tool runs and retrieval quality, not only fixture output.
4. **Review through release:** SHA-bound independent review, phone decisions, approved integration merges, post-merge checks, ordered release plans, infra health/drift and evidence-backed morning reports. Add Jev recommendations with explicit paid opt-in. Verify every approval and acceptance gate, failures/retries and restart recovery.
5. **Complete-product audit:** package a reproducible Mac application; run the original acceptance demo and the new cross-project, Docker DB, design, skill, connector and workflow scenarios. Preserve Apache-2.0, notices, DCO, security docs, license CI, no default telemetry and disabled live outbound integrations. Completion requires current evidence for every original and added requirement; these phases do not narrow the product goal.

## Visual direction

The interface should feel like one connected workbench. Use a quiet project sidebar, a persistent team/status rail and readable work surfaces. Palette: pearl `#f3f6f7`, white `#ffffff`, ink `#18343b`, teal `#087e8b`, mist `#dceef0`, amber `#a15c00`. Use the native system sans-serif for controls and reading, monospace only for commands and SHAs. A connected-agent diagram encodes real message links and status; it is the distinctive visual element. Left-aligned content, visible focus, sentence-case labels and responsive layouts carry the rest.

# Mac app preview

The desktop app uses Tauri 2: a Rust native shell, the existing React dashboard, and the existing TypeScript supervisor with SQLite. Rust manages the app lifecycle and real PTYs. The supervisor keeps ownership of assignments, vendor processes, evidence, and tracker synchronization. This preserves the tested engine while adding native system access.

Rust helps with native process management and avoids shipping a separate Chromium runtime. It does not make vendor inference faster. Transcript pages render at most 200 events at a time, large logs use 128 KiB pages, and the terminal code loads only when opened. Performance claims beyond these design choices need measurements on representative projects. Windows remains a later validation target; the current resource packager and project picker support macOS only.

## Build and launch

Build prerequisites: Node 24+, pnpm, Rust, git, and Apple’s developer tools. Users accept Apple’s tool license themselves. The prepared engine pins Node 24.21.0 and verifies its archive checksum against the official release. It bundles no vendor agent tools or account credentials.

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
cargo fetch --manifest-path packages/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked
pnpm license:check
pnpm desktop:prepare
pnpm desktop:dev
```

For a packaged app:

```sh
pnpm desktop:build
open 'packages/desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/macos/Agent Control Center.app'
```

On a machine with an unaccepted full Xcode installation and working standalone command line tools, prefix Cargo/Tauri build commands with `DEVELOPER_DIR=/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools`. This selects those tools; it does not accept a legal agreement.

The app starts its own daemon and authenticates locally through native IPC. `acc open` is still used for standalone browser access, but the app itself does not need a pasted sign-in link. Closing the window hides it; Quit stops the daemon and native terminals. Detached agent runs retain their restart-safe behavior.

State lives under `~/Library/Application Support/dev.agentcontrolcenter.desktop/`. Each selected configuration has a separate hashed project directory. The offline demo has its own `demo/` directory. The engine is unpacked to a versioned `runtimes/` directory, preserving dependency links. Startup failures are recorded in `daemon.log`.

Without a selected configuration, the app starts a sample repository with **scripted fake agents** and GitHub/Linear import fixtures. These model names, output and usage reports are examples. This mode does not spend subscription usage or connect to either tracker. Use **Open project…** to select a real `control-center.yaml`; stop active runs first.

## Issue imports

The Board’s **Import issues** dialog previews open GitHub or Linear issues, searches their titles/keys/labels, and imports selected issues with provenance and duplicate detection. Imported items get local tracker keys and retain their original source keys and links. Their status changes stay local. The current import flow requires `tracker.type: local`; using an external tracker as the owning tracker is a separate setup.

Configuration declares sources; they remain disabled unless deliberately enabled:

```yaml
tracker: { type: local, key_prefix: ACC }
import_sources:
  - { id: github, name: GitHub, type: github, repo: owner/repository, enabled: false }
  - { id: linear, name: Linear, type: linear, team: ENG, enabled: false }
```

Do not enable a live connection during the offline demo. A live preview uses the user-installed official `gh` CLI or Linear’s public API with a separately configured tracker credential. Vendor subscription credentials are never extracted. The preview currently searches the latest 200 open GitHub issues or 100 Linear issues. Slack import is deferred.

## Work inside the dashboard

Agent Console contains messages, commands, edits, tests, questions, approvals, diffs and durable logs. Claude and Cursor adapters support incremental text where the vendor stream exposes it. Codex’s current `exec` adapter records complete message events; native token streaming and vendor approval handling through Codex app-server remain a separate adapter milestone. Active-run messages for adapters without live input are queued for the next turn. Relay agents still need their vendor surface; they cannot currently satisfy an entirely in-dashboard workflow.

Workspace contains a project/worktree shell and official vendor-login terminals. The terminal is an interactive shell running as the user, not an agent sandbox. Terminal output and keystrokes are not persisted, especially during login. Structured agent-run logs remain durable and redacted. The vendor’s browser OAuth flow may open a browser during sign-in.

Project containers are filtered by the exact Docker Compose project label. Set `project.docker_project` if it differs from `project.name`. Status and the latest 300 log lines are read-only until the human requests and approves a specific start/stop/restart action. Approvals expire after two minutes, cannot be reused, and produce an audit event. Container creation, image pulls, Compose deployment and agent container isolation are not implemented.

## Validation

The offline TypeScript suite covers imports, duplicate provenance across restart, scoped container actions, single-use approvals, native WebSocket tickets, complete large Unicode logs, and transcript history beyond 5000 events. Rust tests cover IPC path restrictions, isolated project directories, PTY execution/resize, and split Unicode output. Mac CI builds the app and runs these checks. This preview is not a notarized public release.

During the local app smoke test, a GitHub fixture was imported, dispatched to the packaged fake Cursor adapter in its own worktree, and finished with a parsed handoff and verified `node --test` evidence. The project terminal also ran the sample repo’s two tests successfully. Live tracker writes, paid model calls and Docker mutations were not used in that test.

# One Answer

One Answer joins committed code, project docs, design contracts, team notes, and the Graphify code graph. Human queries and authenticated agent tools use the same scoped local retrieval. It supplies cited context; it cannot guarantee an answer to every question or override a human decision.

## Intake and freshness

Opening a configured local repository starts background intake automatically. Intake resolves the integration branch to an exact commit; it uses HEAD if that branch does not exist. It reads Git blobs without a checkout, network fetch, project command, dependency install or hook. Uncommitted and untracked work is deliberately excluded and labelled in the UI. A repository without a commit shows an error. A Git/local project creation wizard and indexing of separate active assignment revisions remain subsequent work.

Supported source, documentation, manifest and Docker/config files are extracted into a bounded snapshot. Symlinks, submodules, hidden private folders, credential/env files, certificates, binary files, generated/vendor trees and lockfiles are excluded. Limits are 500 files, 64 KiB per file and 5 MiB total. The dashboard shows included/tracked/excluded counts and marks size-limited results partial. Node package names, dependencies and scripts are extracted declaratively; scripts are never presented as passing tests.

Redaction happens before note, embedding or graph storage. Each file has its source path, revision and redacted content hash. Generated notes use a marked app-owned collection and atomic replacement; intake refuses to overwrite an unowned directory. Source content stays inside fenced Markdown, including content containing its own fences. A private per-project Markdown vault is provided until the user selects an Obsidian vault. Existing unrelated vault notes are never read.

Graphify receives this same redacted snapshot, rather than the live worktree. Its AST extraction invokes no LLM. Graphify must be installed by the user; the app never installs it automatically. Semantic retrieval likewise requires an already-installed local Ollama embedding model and an explicit local search setting. Missing tools/models leave keyword retrieval working and show partial status. Notes, vectors and graph revisions are shown individually; ready requires all configured pipeline stages and no source truncation.

Intake checks for integration changes every minute when graph auto-update is enabled. Re-index project forces a refresh. Generated source integrity and the redaction denylist identity invalidate the cache. Deleted/replaced sources are removed from the retrieval index. Source-line attribution is derived from a daemon-owned registry and content hashes; arbitrary note frontmatter cannot claim a commit. Settings, attribution and progress persist; interrupted intake resumes on restart. Shutdown cancels local model and Graphify requests.

## Agent tools and evidence

`search_context` returns bounded source snippets and optional graph context. `ask_project` returns the same excerpts or local-model interpretation as the dashboard, with citations and intake status. `read_note` provides redacted pages. These sources are untrusted task context, not permission to execute a command or expand scope.

`packages/daemon/test/one-answer.test.ts` covers exact commit extraction versus dirty files; source exclusions/redaction; input validation; count/size bounds; automatic note/vector/graph sync; revision changes; removal of stale passages; authenticated dashboard queries; citation integrity; and restart recovery. Its embedding and Graphify fixtures prove integration behavior, not model quality. The separate real-model retrieval benchmark is documented in [Ask your docs](ask-your-docs.md).

# Mac app preview

The desktop app uses Tauri 2: a Rust native shell, the existing React dashboard, and the existing TypeScript supervisor with SQLite. Rust manages the app lifecycle and real PTYs. The supervisor keeps ownership of assignments, vendor processes, evidence, and tracker synchronization. This preserves the tested engine while adding native system access.

Rust helps with native process management and avoids shipping a separate Chromium runtime. It does not make vendor inference faster. Transcript pages render at most 200 events at a time, large logs use 128 KiB pages, and the terminal code loads only when opened. Performance claims beyond these design choices need measurements on representative projects. Windows remains a later validation target; the current resource packager and project picker support macOS only.

## Build and launch

Build prerequisites: Node 24+, pnpm, Rust, git, and Apple’s developer tools. Users accept Apple’s tool license themselves. The prepared engine pins Node 24.21.0 and verifies its archive checksum against the official release. It bundles no vendor agent tools or account credentials.

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
cargo fetch --manifest-path packages/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked
pnpm license:check
pnpm desktop:prepare
pnpm desktop:dev
```

For a packaged app:

```sh
pnpm desktop:build
open 'packages/desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/macos/Agent Control Center.app'
```

On a machine with an unaccepted full Xcode installation and working standalone command line tools, prefix Cargo/Tauri build commands with `DEVELOPER_DIR=/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools`. This selects those tools; it does not accept a legal agreement.

## Issue imports

The Board’s **Import issues** dialog previews open GitHub or Linear issues, searches their titles/keys/labels, and imports selected issues with provenance and duplicate detection. Imported items get local tracker keys and retain their original source keys and links. Their status changes stay local. The current import flow requires `tracker.type: local`; using an external tracker as the owning tracker is a separate setup.

Configuration declares sources; they remain disabled unless deliberately enabled:

```yaml
tracker: { type: local, key_prefix: ACC }
import_sources:
  - { id: github, name: GitHub, type: github, repo: owner/repository, enabled: false }
  - { id: linear, name: Linear, type: linear, team: ENG, enabled: false }
```

Do not enable a live connection during the offline demo. A live preview uses the user-installed official `gh` CLI or Linear’s public API with a separately configured tracker credential. Agent Console contains messages, commands, edits, tests, questions, approvals, diffs and durable logs. Claude and Cursor adapters support incremental text where the vendor stream exposes it. Active-run messages for adapters without live input are queued for the next turn. Relay agents still need their vendor surface; they cannot currently satisfy an entirely in-dashboard workflow.

## Validation

The offline TypeScript suite covers imports, duplicate provenance across restart, scoped container actions, single-use approvals, native WebSocket tickets, complete large Unicode logs, and transcript history beyond 5000 events. This preview is not a notarized public release.

During the local app smoke test, a GitHub fixture was imported, dispatched to the packaged fake Cursor adapter in its own worktree, and finished with a parsed handoff and verified `node --test` evidence. The project terminal also ran the sample repo’s two tests successfully. Live tracker writes, paid model calls and Docker mutations were not used in that test.

# One Answer

One Answer joins committed code, project docs, design contracts, team notes, and the Graphify code graph. Human queries and authenticated agent tools use the same scoped local retrieval. It supplies cited context; it cannot guarantee an answer to every question or override a human decision.

## Intake and freshness

Opening a configured local repository starts background intake automatically. Intake resolves the integration branch to an exact commit; it uses HEAD if that branch does not exist. It reads Git blobs without a checkout, network fetch, project command, dependency install or hook. Uncommitted and untracked work is deliberately excluded and labelled in the UI. A repository without a commit shows an error. A Git/local project creation wizard and indexing of separate active assignment revisions remain subsequent work.

Supported source, documentation, manifest and Docker/config files are extracted into a bounded snapshot. Symlinks, submodules, hidden private folders, credential/env files, certificates, binary files, generated/vendor trees and lockfiles are excluded. Limits are 500 files, 64 KiB per file and 5 MiB total. The dashboard shows included/tracked/excluded counts and marks size-limited results partial. Node package names, dependencies and scripts are extracted declaratively; scripts are never presented as passing tests.

Redaction happens before note, embedding or graph storage. Each file has its source path, revision and redacted content hash. Generated notes use a marked app-owned collection and atomic replacement; intake refuses to overwrite an unowned directory. Source content stays inside fenced Markdown, including content containing its own fences. A private per-project Markdown vault is provided until the user selects an Obsidian vault. Missing tools/models leave keyword retrieval working and show partial status. Intake checks for integration changes every minute when graph auto-update is enabled. Re-index project forces a refresh. Generated source integrity and the redaction denylist identity invalidate the cache. Deleted/replaced sources are removed from the retrieval index. # Mac app preview

The desktop app uses Tauri 2: a Rust native shell, the existing React dashboard, and the existing TypeScript supervisor with SQLite. Rust manages the app lifecycle and real PTYs. The supervisor keeps ownership of assignments, vendor processes, evidence, and tracker synchronization. This preserves the tested engine while adding native system access.

Rust helps with native process management and avoids shipping a separate Chromium runtime. It does not make vendor inference faster. Transcript pages render at most 200 events at a time, large logs use 128 KiB pages, and the terminal code loads only when opened. Performance claims beyond these design choices need measurements on representative projects. Windows remains a later validation target; the current resource packager and the project and folder pickers support macOS only.

## Build and launch

Build prerequisites: Node 24+, pnpm, Rust, git, and Apple’s developer tools. Users accept Apple’s tool license themselves. The prepared engine pins Node 24.21.0 and verifies its archive checksum against the official release. It bundles no vendor agent tools or account credentials.

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
cargo fetch --manifest-path packages/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked
pnpm license:check
pnpm desktop:prepare
pnpm desktop:dev
```

For a packaged app:

```sh
pnpm desktop:build
open 'packages/desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/macos/Agent Control Center.app'
```

The app starts one daemon per project and authenticates to each locally through native IPC. `acc open` is still used for standalone browser access, but the app itself does not need a pasted sign-in link. Closing the window hides it; Quit asks every project's daemon to shut down gracefully and closes native terminals. Detached agent runs retain their restart-safe behavior.

State lives under `~/Library/Application Support/dev.agentcontrolcenter.desktop/`. Each project has a separate directory named by the hash of its configuration path (`projects/<id>/state`), holding its event database, worktrees, One Answer index, generated database files and secrets. The supervisor keeps ownership of assignments, vendor processes, evidence, and tracker synchronization. This preserves the tested engine while adding native system access.

Rust helps with native process management and avoids shipping a separate Chromium runtime. It does not make vendor inference faster. Transcript pages render at most 200 events at a time, large logs use 128 KiB pages, and the terminal code loads only when opened. Performance claims beyond these design choices need measurements on representative projects. Windows remains a later validation target; the current resource packager and the project and folder pickers support macOS only.

## Build and launch

Build prerequisites: Node 24+, pnpm, Rust, git, and Apple’s developer tools. Users accept Apple’s tool license themselves. The prepared engine pins Node 24.21.0 and verifies its archive checksum against the official release. It bundles no vendor agent tools or account credentials.

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
cargo fetch --manifest-path packages/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked
pnpm license:check
pnpm desktop:prepare
pnpm desktop:dev
```

For a packaged app:

```sh
pnpm desktop:build
open 'packages/desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/macos/Agent Control Center.app'
```

On a machine with an unaccepted full Xcode installation and working standalone command line tools, prefix Cargo/Tauri build commands with `DEVELOPER_DIR=/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools`. This selects those tools; it does not accept a legal agreement.

The app starts one daemon per project and authenticates to each locally through native IPC. `acc open` is still used for standalone browser access, but the app itself does not need a pasted sign-in link. Closing the window hides it; Quit asks every project's daemon to shut down gracefully and closes native terminals. Detached agent runs retain their restart-safe behavior.

State lives under `~/Library/Application Support/dev.agentcontrolcenter.desktop/`. Each project has a separate directory named by the hash of its configuration path (`projects/<id>/state`), holding its event database, worktrees, One Answer index, generated database files and secrets. The offline demo has its own `demo/` directory. The engine is unpacked to a versioned `runtimes/` directory, preserving dependency links. Startup failures are recorded in `daemon.log`.

## Projects

`projects.json` (owner-only) is the durable project registry: name, configuration, exact repository root, onboarding scan, the open project and which engines were running. A corrupt registry is kept aside, not overwritten; a `selected-config` file from earlier builds is migrated. One repository maps to one project.

**Projects → Add a local repository** opens the macOS folder picker and scans the chosen repository root without running its scripts: Git state, frameworks, package manager, declared checks, Compose services and Dockerfiles. A subfolder of a repository, the home folder, system folders and credential folders are refused. If the repository has a `control-center.yaml` whose `project.repo` resolves to the same root, it is used; otherwise a private configuration is generated under `project-configs/` and nothing is written into the repository. A folder without Git gets a reviewable `git init` step that runs only after approval; a repository without commits is added with “needs first commit”, and uncommitted changes are reported as excluded, so One Answer never claims to have indexed work that is not at a Git revision.

**Clone from a Git URL** prepares the exact `git clone` command (hooks, submodules, credential helpers and `ext::` transports disabled). It reaches the network only after the human approves that command; the approval is bound to its digest, expires after two minutes and works once. URLs with embedded credentials are refused. SSH URLs may use the user's SSH agent; HTTPS credential helpers and prompts are off, so private HTTPS repositories need an SSH URL.

Switching projects changes which engine the window shows. Other projects' supervisors and agent runs keep going; returning shows their live dashboard and logs. Every native request names its project and is routed to that project's own connection and token; a response that arrives after a switch is dropped. Per project, **Stop runs** engages that project's kill switch and **Stop engine** shuts its daemon down. **Kill switch: all projects** engages every running project's kill switch. Engines that were running at Quit restart on the next launch and reattach their detached runs. Before each start the app re-checks that the configuration still points at the registered repository and that the daemon serves it. A daemon left by a crash is stopped only if its command line proves it is that project's engine.

The Board’s **Import issues** dialog previews open GitHub or Linear issues, searches their titles/keys/labels, and imports selected issues with provenance and duplicate detection. Configuration declares sources; they remain disabled unless deliberately enabled:

```yaml
tracker: { type: local, key_prefix: ACC }
import_sources:
  - { id: github, name: GitHub, type: github, repo: owner/repository, enabled: false }
  - { id: linear, name: Linear, type: linear, team: ENG, enabled: false }
```
